pages.title: Doctrine of Basic Structure
pages.summary: The Doctrine of Basic Structure is a judicial innovation allowing the Supreme Court of India to challenge constitutional amendments. Its evolution arose from the context of contradictory principles between Part III and Part IV of the Constitution.

pages.title: Part III, Part IV, and Champakam Dorairajan
pages.summary: Part III guarantees enforceable Fundamental Rights based on liberalism, whereas Part IV contains non-enforceable Directive Principles aimed at establishing an egalitarian society through a socialist vision. The Champakam Dorairajan case of 1950 marked the first dispute between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles.

pages.title: Champakam Dorairajan Case: Issue and Judicial Solution
pages.summary: The petitioner challenged Madras's reservation policy for violating the Right to Equality, creating a dilemma between safeguarding Fundamental Rights and advancing Directive Principles under Article 46. The judiciary resolved this by creatively interpreting the term 'law' in Article 13(2) as referring only to ordinary laws, not constitutional amendments.

pages.title: First Amendment Act and Shankari Prasad Case
pages.summary: Following judicial observations that Fundamental Rights could only be abridged via constitutional amendments, the government enacted the 1st Amendment Act of 1951. In the Shankari Prasad case and subsequent rulings like Sajjan Singh, the Supreme Court upheld the validity of these amendments.

pages.title: Golaknath Case and 24th Amendment Act
pages.summary: In the Golaknath case (1967), the Supreme Court applied prospective overruling and held that the term 'law' in Article 13(2) includes amendments, preventing Parliament from abridging Fundamental Rights. In response, the government passed the 24th Amendment Act of 1971 to explicitly exclude Article 368 amendments from Article 13.

pages.title: 25th Amendment Act and Kesavananda Bharati Case
pages.summary: The 25th Amendment Act of 1971 added Article 31(c) to protect laws implementing Articles 39(b) and 39(c) from being declared void under Article 13. In the Kesavananda Bharati case (1973), the Supreme Court upheld the 24th and 25th Amendments while establishing the Doctrine of Basic Structure.

pages.title: Meaning and Reception of Basic Structure Doctrine
pages.summary: The Doctrine of Basic Structure allows Parliament to amend the Constitution to any extent provided the amendment does not destroy its basic structure. The historic ruling produced mixed reactions regarding judicial overreach versus constitutional protection and was decided by a 7–6 majority among 13 judges.

pages.title: Minerva Mills Case and 42nd Amendment Act
pages.summary: In the Minerva Mills case (1980), the Supreme Court first applied the Basic Structure doctrine to strike down Articles 368(4) and 368(5) introduced by the 42nd Amendment Act. The Court also restored Article 31(c) protection to only Articles 39(b) and 39(c), rather than all Directive Principles.

pages.title: I.R. Coelho Case and Zia Mody Evaluation
pages.summary: In I.R. Coelho (2007), the Supreme Court held that the Basic Structure doctrine applies to laws inducted into the Ninth Schedule on or after April 24, 1973. According to author Zia Mody, the doctrine remains contested but served as a crucial safeguard against authoritarianism in India.

pages.title: Basic Structure Debates and FRs versus DPSPs
pages.summary: Notes discuss arguments for retaining the Basic Structure doctrine as a safety valve despite criticisms that it prioritizes metaphysics over literal constitutional text. The page also outlines the historical friction between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles arising from conflicting liberal and socialist philosophies.

pages.title: FRs and DPSPs Harmony and Historical Separation
pages.summary: Judicial decisions and constitutional amendments alternately disrupted and restored harmony between Part III and Part IV, which are complementary rather than mutually exclusive. Both categories of rights were originally integrated in the Motilal Nehru report and B.N. Rao's scheme but separated due to resource constraints, with Ambedkar noting Directive Principles carry political sanction.

pages.title: DPSPs via Article 21 and Right to Equality
pages.summary: The judiciary elevated many Directive Principles to Fundamental Rights through liberal interpretation of Article 21, with Granville Austin viewing the Preamble, FRs, and DPs as an indivisible integrated scheme. The notes then introduce the Right to Equality, citing Dworkin's view of equality as a sovereign virtue linked to human dignity and prioritized over freedom.

pages.title: Substantive Equality and Articles 14 to 18
pages.summary: The Constitution embraces substantive and differentiated equality through affirmative action to address India-specific inequalities, prohibiting discrimination by both the state and private persons. Articles 14 through 18 permit reasonable classification, enable positive discrimination, ensure a level playing field for weaker sections, address untouchability, and abolish hereditary titles.

flashcards.front: Why does the Doctrine of Basic Structure make the Supreme Court of India the strongest court in the world according to the notes?
flashcards.back: No other court, including the US Supreme Court, has the power to challenge constitutional amendments. Through this doctrine, the Indian judiciary can challenge provisions added by amendment, assuming the role of the constituent assembly despite being the least representative and accountable organ.

flashcards.front: What creative interpretation of Article 13(2) was adopted by the Supreme Court in the Champakam Dorairajan case?
flashcards.back: The Supreme Court distinguished between ordinary law and a constitutional amendment. It held that the term 'law' used in Article 13(2) meant only ordinary law and did not include constitutional amendments.

flashcards.front: What was the judicial ruling in the Golaknath case (1967) regarding constitutional amendments and Fundamental Rights?
flashcards.back: The Supreme Court held that the term 'law' under Article 13(2) includes constitutional amendments, meaning Fundamental Rights cannot be abridged even by an amendment. It marked the first application of the doctrine of prospective overruling and is considered the first instance of judicial activism.

flashcards.front: What provision did the 25th Amendment Act, 1971 introduce through Article 31(C)?
flashcards.back: It added Article 31(C), stipulating that any law aiming to implement the objectives found in Articles 39(B) and 39(C) shall not be declared null and void on the basis of Article 13.

flashcards.front: What is the core logic of the Doctrine of Basic Structure formulated in the Kesavananda Bharati case?
flashcards.back: Parliament has the power to amend the Constitution to whatever extent, but such amendment cannot destroy the Constitution's basic structure. The judiciary drew a distinction between amending the Constitution and rewriting it so that the original document is not lost.

flashcards.front: Which provisions introduced by the 42nd Amendment Act were struck down in the Minerva Mills case (1980)?
flashcards.back: The Supreme Court declared Article 368(4) and Article 368(5) null and void for removing judicial review and creating unlimited amending power. It also struck down the amendment to Article 31(C) that extended immunity to all directives, restoring the position under the 25th Amendment.

flashcards.front: What did the Supreme Court rule regarding the Ninth Schedule in the I.R. Coelho case (2007)?
flashcards.back: The Supreme Court held that the Doctrine of Basic Structure can be applied to examine the constitutional validity of laws placed under the Ninth Schedule. However, this review applies only to laws inducted into the Ninth Schedule on and after April 24, 1973.

flashcards.front: How does Zia Mody evaluate the Doctrine of Basic Structure in 'The Ten Judgements That Changed India'?
flashcards.back: Zia Mody notes that while the doctrine remains academically contested, it proved to be a practical blessing in disguise. It prevented India from sliding into authoritarianism like other Third World nations, showing that uncertain democracy is preferable over certain tyranny.

flashcards.front: Why were Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles separated in the Constitution according to Sir B.N. Rau?
flashcards.back: According to Constituent Assembly adviser B.N. Rau, both sets of rights were originally presented as an integrated scheme but were later separated because the country lacked resources. Making social and economic rights immediately enforceable in court would have precipitated a constitutional crisis.

answers.question: Critically examine the evolution and significance of the Doctrine of Basic Structure in Indian constitutionalism. Does it act as a vital safety valve against authoritarianism?
answers.intro: The Doctrine of Basic Structure is a unique judicial innovation by the Supreme Court of India, designed to prevent Parliament from rewriting the original Constitution under Article 368 while safeguarding democratic constitutionalism from authoritarian tendencies.
body: In Shankari Prasad (1951) and Sajjan Singh, the Supreme Court conceded broad amending power to Parliament under Article 368, but reversed this in Golaknath (1967) through prospective overruling, holding that Fundamental Rights cannot be abridged even by constitutional amendments.

The landmark Kesavananda Bharati case (1973) resolved this standoff through a 7:6 majority, upholding the 24th and 25th Amendments while establishing that Article 368 grants the power to amend, but not to rewrite or destroy the Constitution's basic structure.

In Minerva Mills (1980), the court struck down clauses (4) and (5) of Article 368 added by the 42nd Amendment, holding that conferring absolute amending power onto Parliament would destroy judicial review and dismantle the basic structure itself.

Extended to Ninth Schedule laws post-1973 in I.R. Coelho (2007), writer Zia Mody in 'The Ten Judgements That Changed India' highlights that despite academic criticisms of judicial overreach, the doctrine remains a vital safety valve, proving that uncertain democracy is preferable over certain tyranny.
scholars: Zia Mody ('The Ten Judgements That Changed India')
answers.conclusion: Though criticized for judicial metaphysics and vagueness, keeping the basic structure open-ended acts as an essential constitutional safety valve, successfully harmonizing parliamentary authority with constitutional supremacy in India's evolving democratic landscape.

answers.question: Analyze the evolving relationship between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles of State Policy from conflict to complementarity. How has the judiciary established constitutional harmony between the two?
answers.intro: The relationship between Part III (Fundamental Rights) and Part IV (Directive Principles) reflects the constitutional synthesis of liberal civil liberties and socialist socio-economic equality, evolving from initial judicial friction toward mutual complementarity.
body: As constitutional adviser B.N. Rau and the Motilal Nehru Report (1928) revealed, both categories of rights originally formed an integrated scheme, separated solely due to initial resource scarcity; as Dr. B.R. Ambedkar observed, Directives carry vital political sanction despite lacking immediate legal enforceability.

In Champakam Dorairajan (1950), the Supreme Court sought harmonious construction but maintained the primacy of Fundamental Rights, an approach drastically hardened in Golaknath (1967) where judicial activism destroyed harmony by holding that constitutional amendments could not touch Fundamental Rights.

Parliament sought to establish harmony through the 25th Amendment by inserting Article 31(C), which the Supreme Court upheld in Kesavananda Bharati (1973), recognizing that laws implementing socio-economic directives under Articles 39(B) and 39(C) must be shielded from challenge under Article 13.

In Minerva Mills (1980), the court struck down the 42nd Amendment's total subordination of rights, restoring equilibrium; as Granville Austin emphasized, the Preamble, Fundamental Rights, and Directives together constitute the indivisible soul of the Constitution and operate as complementary partners.
answers.conclusion: Ultimately, Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles are complementary rather than exclusionary. Through liberal interpretation of Article 21 and progressive amendments like Article 21A, the Indian judiciary continues to transform socio-economic directives into enforceable fundamental rights.
